name: Guardian genius crossword No 159
preamble: Ten solutions contain a slice of 2, not included in the wordplay of their clues.

solutions.check: grid and clues read from the Guardian's printable PDF, its numbering matching the clue list; each light's entry one fifteensquared prints for it, the only choice of them whose crossings all agree; an entry not its answer carries the answer as its alteration's `from`

clue.text: Fodder providing last part of answer is concealed in second half of clue

indicators.note: the final part of a word is its closing letter, so only the end of the next word is kept
something concealed in a place sits inside it, so one piece goes within the other
the second half of a four-letter word is its final pair of letters, so only those are kept

blocks.note: a slice of the beef at 2 down, supplied by the preamble and not by the clue
the second half of this four-letter word
the final letter of this word

explanation.surface: A self-referential instruction that seems to tell the solver where to find animal feed inside the clue itself.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds only URE; the preamble's slice PAST from PASTRAMI goes in front to make PASTURE.
explanation.definitionFit: Pasture is grassland grazed by livestock, so the growing grass serves as animal feed.

clue.text: History records agricultural methods introduced originally for beef production

indicators.note: what comes originally is what comes first, so each word gives its opening letter

blocks.note: history is what is past
the opening letters of these four words

explanation.surface: A historical study of farming practices that were brought in to raise beef cattle.
explanation.walkthrough: This answer is the '2' of the preamble: ten other answers contain a slice of it.
explanation.definitionFit: Pastrami is a seasoned, smoked cured meat usually made from brisket, so it is something produced from cattle.

clue.text: Does lover maybe represent a bit of a catch?

indicators.note: to re-present something is to present it afresh in a new arrangement

blocks.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: Asks whether a boyfriend counts as a good catch in the romantic sense.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Catch' suggests an eligible partner, but here it means a haul of fish.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dover sole is a prized flatfish, so one would be part of a fisherman's haul.

clue.text: Star is keen to play second fiddle perhaps in setting up of festival

indicators.note: one group of letters is placed in another, so it sits inside it
in a down clue, setting something up raises it, so the word is read from bottom to top

blocks.note: avid means eager
to bow is to defer, as one playing second fiddle does
Eid is a Muslim festival

explanation.surface: A celebrity is happy to take a supporting role at some music festival.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fiddle' suggests violin playing and a bow, but the bow here is the deferential bending kind.
explanation.definitionFit: David Bowie was a hugely famous rock singer, a star of music.

clue.text: France's wingers attack

indicators.note: wingers play on the flanks, so only the two edge letters are kept

blocks.note: a slice of the beef at 2 down, supplied by the preamble and not by the clue
the edge letters of the country name

explanation.surface: French wide players launching an attack in a football match.
explanation.walkthrough: This is one of the ten answers holding a slice of 2 down that the wordplay leaves out.
explanation.definitionFit: To strafe is to attack with gunfire from low-flying aircraft.

clue.text: Revolutionary design for nurturing surrounding landscape?

indicators.note: a revolution turns things round, so the letters run backwards
the words nurture, or hold within, the letters wanted across their join

blocks.note: a slice of the beef at 2 down, supplied by the preamble and not by the clue
the fifth letter, where the run of letters held across the two words starts
the closing letter, next in the run
the opening letter, ending the run of three

explanation.surface: Suggests a radical new scheme for raising crops or livestock.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay gives only FNG; the slice RAMI goes after its first letter to make FRAMING.
explanation.definitionFit: Framing is the border put round a picture, such as a painted landscape; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Soldier and mistress almost say: "I always lie"

indicators.note: almost means not quite all, so the final letter is dropped

blocks.note: a paratrooper
an old word for a mistress

explanation.surface: A soldier and his lover, one of whom confesses to being a habitual liar.
explanation.definitionFit: The liar's statement is a classic self-contradiction: if it is true, it is false, an example of a logical puzzle.

clue.text: Nationalist queen leading support for Clydesdale?

blocks.note: a slice of the beef at 2 down, supplied by the preamble and not by the clue
Elizabeth Regina
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A Scottish nationalist monarch at the front of a campaign of backing for the Clyde region.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Leading' places the queen before the nationalist; a Clydesdale is a breed of heavy draught horse, not the Scottish valley.
explanation.definitionFit: The pastern is the part of a horse's leg between fetlock and hoof, which helps bear its weight.

clue.text: Fan confusion following loss of the guitarist

indicators.note: losing something means it is taken away, so the named word goes

blocks.note: to muddy the waters is to stir up confusion
taken as written

explanation.surface: A fan in disarray after the death of a favourite musician.
explanation.definitionFit: Muddy Waters was the stage name of an influential American blues singer and guitar player.

clue.text: Last time to act having gone bust?

indicators.note: something that has gone is no longer there, so the letter is removed

blocks.note: an act of parliament
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: The final chance to do something before going bankrupt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Last' says which T goes: the final one in STATUTE, not the first.
explanation.definitionFit: A bust is a sculpture of head and shoulders, one example of a sculpted figure; the question mark flags the example.

clue.text: Incensed by liberal puritanism wanting sex

indicators.note: wanting means lacking, so these letters are missing
liberal means free and loose, so the letters are rearranged freely

blocks.note: taken as written
it is a coy word for sex appeal

explanation.surface: Someone outraged by a permissive form of puritanism that lacks any sex.
explanation.definitionFit: Up in arms is an idiom for being angrily protesting, which matches being enraged.

clue.text: Women fish for compliments? Not this one!

definitions.note: the definition is negative: something that is not a compliment

blocks.note: American slang for women
a freshwater fish of the carp family

explanation.surface: Women fishing for compliments are told they will not get one.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fish for' looks like one phrase; split it, and fish gives the letters while the rest defines.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadside is a fierce verbal attack, the very opposite of praise.

clue.text: Dummy's not too bright we hear

indicators.note: what we hear is spoken, so the sound matters, not the spelling

blocks.note: a faint light is not too bright

explanation.surface: A gibe that a stupid person is not very clever.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Not too bright' reads as dim-witted; it is a dim light.
explanation.definitionFit: A dummy in sport is a pretended move to deceive an opponent, which is a mock attack.

clue.text: Dead soldiers described by short note covering two sides

indicators.note: to describe a shape is to draw round it, so one piece goes round the other
cut short means the last letter is dropped

blocks.note: the late means the dead
Royal Artillery
a bill is a written note or account

explanation.surface: Fallen soldiers listed on a brief memo.
explanation.definitionFit: Bilateral means involving or affecting both sides, as in a two-party agreement.

clue.text: Bedroom action?

blocks.note: surface reading: something more intimate in the bedroom
setter's reading: a playful battle fought with bedding

explanation.walkthrough: The suggestive phrase points to romance, but the action is children battering each other with what lies on the bed.
explanation.definitionFit: A game where people swing soft cushions from the bed at each other is literally action in a bedroom.

clue.text: Browbeating, nonetheless, contributes to unnatural death

indicators.note: unnatural means not in the normal state, so the letters are rearranged

blocks.note: but means nevertheless
taken as written

explanation.surface: Bullying behaviour that still leads to a suspicious death.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Browbeating' means bullying, but read literally it is beating with the brow.
explanation.definitionFit: A headbutt is a blow struck with the forehead, literally a beating delivered by the brow.

clue.text: The old Democratic leader was unfaithful

indicators.note: a leader comes at the front, so only the opening letter is taken

blocks.note: a slice of the beef at 2 down, supplied by the preamble and not by the clue
ye is an archaic form of the
opening letter

explanation.surface: A former Democratic party leader who cheated on his spouse.
explanation.walkthrough: The wordplay builds only YED; the slice STRA goes in front.
explanation.definitionFit: To stray is to wander from a partner, a common euphemism for committing adultery.

clue.text: Amount of money made on site

blocks.note: re means on the subject of
a venue is a site for an event

explanation.surface: Describes money earned at a location, like takings on site.
explanation.definitionFit: Revenue is income, the money a business or government takes in.

clue.text: Tube from Heathrow terminal

indicators.note: a terminal letter is one at the end, so only the closing one is kept

blocks.note: a slice of the beef at 2 down, supplied by the preamble and not by the clue
closing letter

explanation.surface: Taking the London Underground (the Tube) from an airport terminal.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tube' and 'terminal' paint London transport; Heathrow is London's main airport.
explanation.definitionFit: A drinking straw is a thin hollow pipe for sipping liquid.

clue.text: Walsall entertains a couple of stars

indicators.note: the place name entertains, or holds inside it, a pair of letters to be picked out

blocks.note: a slice of the beef at 2 down, supplied by the preamble and not by the clue
the second letter, first of the pair held inside the town name
the third letter, second of the pair

explanation.surface: Walsall, a town in the English West Midlands, plays host to two celebrities.
explanation.walkthrough: 'A couple of stars' reads as two celebrities, but the couple belongs to the wordplay and 'of stars' is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Astral is an adjective meaning relating to the heavenly bodies in the sky.

clue.text: Have a great time turning 13

indicators.note: turning round makes the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a slice of the beef at 2 down, supplied by the preamble and not by the clue
slang for great
standard abbreviation

explanation.surface: A cheerful wish to enjoy oneself on reaching the age of thirteen.
explanation.walkthrough: '13' looks like a birthday but refers to the answer at 13 across. A slice of 2 down, absent from the wordplay, starts the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: A feint is a deceptive move, and a stratagem is a scheme or trick to outwit an opponent.

clue.text: See 4
Move fast to make fast pony

blocks.note: to dart is to move quickly
to moor a boat is to make it fast

explanation.surface: Urging speed to get a pony to go quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Fast' is used twice in different senses: quick, then secured.
explanation.definitionFit: The Dartmoor is a breed of small hardy horse from the moorland in Devon, England.

clue.text: It's symbolic when other people repeatedly take sides in brawl

indicators.note: to take something in is to hold it inside
the sides of a word are its outer letters

blocks.note: 'em is short for them, given twice
outer letters

explanation.surface: Onlookers repeatedly picking sides in a fight is said to mean something.
explanation.definitionFit: An emblem is a badge or sign standing for an idea, so it is a symbolic thing.

clue.text: Conclusion of tale in small volume of Potter's work

indicators.note: the conclusion of a word is its closing letter
one piece placed in another sits inside it

blocks.note: closing letter
cubic centimetres
a slice of the beef at 2 down, supplied by the preamble and not by the clue

explanation.surface: The end of a story in a slim book by Beatrix Potter.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Potter' suggests Beatrix or Harry, but it is a maker of pots. The wordplay gives CEC; the slice RAMI goes before the last C.
explanation.definitionFit: Ceramic is fired clay, the stuff a pottery maker produces.

clue.text: Though not even turned 18, he's a famous scientist

indicators.note: not means without, so the following word is taken out
turned round means the letters run the other way

blocks.note: a slice of the beef at 2 down, supplied by the preamble and not by the clue
the answer at 18 down
taken as written

explanation.surface: A prodigy who became a famous scientist before even reaching eighteen.
explanation.walkthrough: '18' looks like an age but refers to the answer at 18 down. 'Not even' looks like odd letters but removes the word itself.
explanation.definitionFit: Louis Pasteur was the French chemist known for pasteurisation and vaccines, a celebrated man of science.
